This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Is it true that, for any $a\in\mathbb{Z}$, there are infinitely many $n$ such that\[\phi(n) \mid n+a?\]
#828: [Er83]
number theory
A conjecture of Graham. Lehmer has conjectured that $\phi(n)\mid n-1$ if and only if $n$ is prime. It is an easy exercise to show that $\phi(n) \mid n$ if and only if $n=2^a3^b$ for some $a,b\geq 0$.
This is discussed in problem B37 of Guy's collection [Gu04]. 
Additional thanks to: Torlach

 An elementary remark. If $b$ is odd and $\newline$ $n > 2$ satisfies $\phi(n) \mid n + b$, then $n$ is odd, and for any $r \ge 1, 2^rn$ satisfies $\phi(2^r n) \mid 2^r n + 2^r b$. Consequently, to resolve the conjecture for all integers a, it is both necessary and sufficient to prove it for all odd shifts.
